books.section: Topic 6.6 The Rise of Industrial Capitalism
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

options.misconception: Tarbell writes about a business combination, not a partnership with the government.
options.text: A partnership between Standard Oil and the federal government

options.misconception: Background: oil workers did not form the combination; the companies did.
options.text: A group of oil workers who joined a union
The group of oil companies joined under Standard Oil’s control

options.misconception: Background: Standard Oil worked with railroads, but the combination was the oil trust itself.
options.text: A merger of Standard Oil with the railroads

rationales.A: The government investigated Standard Oil; it did not join it.
rationales.B: Background: the combination joined companies, not workers. Workers and unions belong to the labor story.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Standard Oil was a trust, formed when the stockholders of many oil companies put their shares under one board’s control.
rationales.D: Background: Standard Oil made deals with railroads, but the trust joined oil companies, not railroads.
rationales.general:
Use the passage and the word’s meaning.
1. Tarbell calls Standard Oil a combination that makes huge profits.
2. Background from the books: a trust joined many companies in one industry under a single board.
3. Standard Oil was the best-known trust, built by joining oil companies.
4. So “the combination” is the joined companies, not a partner or a union.
Remember: when a passage uses a business term, match it to the business form.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: In the passage, what does Tarbell mean by “the combination”?

stimulus.source_note: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company, Vol. 2, Chapter 18 (1904), public domain.
stimulus.text: “The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year, or nearly fifty per cent. on its capitalisation, a sum which capitalised at five per cent. would give $900,000,000. Of course this is not all that the combination makes in a year. It allows an annual average of 5.77 per cent. for deficit, and it carries always an ample reserve fund.”
